entry.title: Reconstructing Soft Arms in Real Time with Neural Networks
entry.content:
A soft robot needs to know its shape while it moves. A few tracked markers can tell us where selected cross-sections are and how they are oriented, but the arm bends, twists, and stretches continuously between those observations. Recovering that continuous deformation is already difficult. Doing it quickly enough to keep up with motion adds another challenge.

In Seeing How Soft Arms Deform: From Camera Images to Six Strain Fields, I described our earlier method for combining camera measurements with Cosserat rod mechanics. It reconstructs the arm's posture and strain fields by repeatedly solving an optimization problem. The results reveal deformations that an outline alone cannot show, but the calculation can require thousands of iterations for a single frame.

Our follow-up paper, A Neural Network-Based Framework for Fast and Smooth Posture Reconstruction of a Soft Continuum Arm, addresses that bottleneck. Tixian Wang and I, together with our collaborators, develop a neural network that learns the mapping from sparse marker poses to a continuous strain representation. Rod mechanics then turns those strains into the reconstructed arm.

The reported reconstruction benchmark is more than five orders of magnitude faster than the earlier forward-backward algorithm, with comparable normalized objective loss. The central idea is to move the repeated computational effort into training, so a new measurement can be processed with a network evaluation and a spatial integration.

Reconstruction in action

From an optimization problem to a learned map

The earlier approach asks: which smooth deformation best balances mechanical energy, agreement with observations, and the chosen regularization? It integrates the arm's pose from base to tip, propagates a costate backward, and updates the strain description until the optimization converges.

Each measurement set therefore defines a reconstruction problem. Across many frames, these problems have a common structure: the input is a collection of marker poses, and the output is a set of strain fields. We train a network to approximate that input-output relationship.

The input is already a three-dimensional pose estimate. Each marker contributes its position and two perpendicular unit vectors, or directors, describing its orientation. These supply nine numbers per marker; the remaining director follows from orthonormality. The camera or motion-capture system provides these measurements before the network runs.

The output is more subtle. A neural network produces a finite vector, while bending, twist, shear, and stretch vary along the entire arm. We need a way to represent those continuous fields with a small number of numbers.

A small set of patterns describes continuous strain

We begin with simulated motions of the arm and collect the strain profiles that occur along its length. Principal component analysis (PCA) identifies a compact set of spatial patterns that captures the main variations in each strain component.

For strain component $i$, the approximation takes the form

$$ \hat\varepsilon^i(s)=\bar\varepsilon^i_0(s) +\sum_{j=1}^{N_b}\alpha^i_j\bar\varepsilon^i_j(s). $$

Here, $s$ measures location along the reference length, $\bar\varepsilon^i_0$ is the mean strain profile, and the remaining $\bar\varepsilon^i_j$ are basis functions obtained from the simulated data. The coefficients $\alpha^i_j$ tell us how much of each pattern to use. The network predicts those coefficients.

For the simulated octopus arm, four components for each of six strain modes give 24 network outputs. Those 24 values specify strain profiles along the whole arm. This compact representation also limits which deformations the estimator can express: its vocabulary comes from the simulated motions used to construct the basis.

Once the strains are known, we reconstruct position $\mathbf x(s)$ and orientation $Q(s)$ using the Cosserat rod kinematics:

$$ \frac{d\mathbf x}{ds}=Q\boldsymbol\nu, \qquad \frac{dQ}{ds}=Q[\boldsymbol\kappa]_\times. $$

The vector $\boldsymbol\kappa$ contains two bending strains and twist; $\boldsymbol\nu$ contains two shear strains and stretch. The matrix $[\boldsymbol\kappa]_\times$ represents taking a cross product with $\boldsymbol\kappa$. With the base pose specified, integrating these equations connects the predicted local deformations into a complete posture.

Training with mechanics and marker measurements

Collecting dense, accurate strain measurements from a physical soft arm would be expensive. Generating thousands of target reconstructions with the previous optimization algorithm would also carry a substantial computational cost.

Instead, we expand the simulated dataset by sampling strain coefficients from distributions fitted to the PCA results. We integrate the sampled strains into arm postures, extract virtual marker poses at the chosen locations, and add Gaussian noise to represent measurement uncertainty.

During training, the network receives these noisy poses and predicts strain coefficients. Its reconstruction is scored using

$$ J(\hat q;\mathcal M) =U(\hat q)+\frac{\eta}{2}\Phi(\hat q;\mathcal M). $$

Here, $\hat q$ is the reconstructed posture, $\mathcal M$ is the marker measurement set, $U$ is the arm's potential energy, and $\Phi$ penalizes disagreement with measured positions and orientations. The weight $\eta$ controls the balance between the two terms. The rod equations constrain how strain becomes posture, while the energy term supplies a mechanical preference among possible reconstructions.

This is what the paper calls unsupervised learning: the training loss does not require target strain labels. The method still uses a simulator to build its basis and synthetic training inputs, and it depends on a mechanical model. Learning takes place through the energy and observation costs evaluated on each predicted arm.

How much faster is reconstruction?

The networks are small multilayer perceptrons with two hidden layers. The octopus model uses layers of 128 and 64 neurons; the physical-arm model uses 32 and 16. Training and inference were performed on a laptop with an Intel Core i7-12700H processor and 16 GB of memory, without a dedicated GPU.

Figure 3 compares the learned reconstruction with the previous forward-backward algorithm. Five orders of magnitude corresponds to a factor of 100,000. This comparison measures the reconstruction calculation once marker poses are available; camera acquisition, tracking, communication, and any later control calculation have their own timing costs.

The accuracy comparison uses the reconstruction objective, normalized by the measurement weight and number of markers. It supports the claim that the speed improvement preserves a comparable level of fit under that objective. The separate demonstrations below show what the resulting shapes and strains look like.

Recovering six strain fields in a simulated octopus arm

The first testbed is a 20 cm tapered muscular arm simulated with COOMM and Elastica. Energy-shaping control drives reaching motions toward 27 targets distributed through a three-dimensional workspace. Eight virtual markers provide the observations.

The network receives 72 input values and predicts the 24 coefficients representing all six strain modes. In simulation, the underlying strain fields are available, so we can compare the reconstructed profiles with the simulator's ground truth.

For all 27 reaching trajectories, the time-averaged reconstruction error is below the reported 0.2% level. This percentage has a specific definition: it is the mean marker-pose mismatch, combining squared position differences normalized by arm length squared and squared orientation-matrix differences normalized by eight.

It therefore measures how well the reconstructed poses agree with the observations. It does not translate directly into a position error in millimeters or a percentage error in every strain field. The strain comparisons provide additional, separate evidence about the deformation recovered between markers.

From simulation to a physical pneumatic arm

The second testbed is a 30 cm BR² pneumatic manipulator. Its three pressure inputs produce bending and twisting in either direction. Three ring markers carry reflective tags, and a Vicon motion-capture system supplies their poses at 100 Hz. A complementary filter stabilizes the pose readings before reconstruction.

The training basis comes from COBRA, a simulator for the BR² arm. For this experiment, the model assumes the arm is inextensible and unshearable, so the learned variables are the three angular strains: two bends and twist. Three PCA components per angular strain give nine network outputs from 27 inputs.

The experiment reconstructs the arm in real time as it moves through bending, combined bending and twisting, and nearly straight twisting. The repeated trajectories and error curves show consistent behavior across three cycles.

This demonstrates transfer from simulation-generated training data to a physical manipulator. The hardware evaluation compares against measured marker poses and visually checks the reconstructed shape; it does not provide independent measurements of strain everywhere along the physical arm. The six-mode reconstruction is demonstrated in the octopus simulation, while the BR² experiment uses the more restricted model described above.

What “fast and smooth” makes possible

The extension preserves the central aim of the earlier vision-based work: infer continuous deformation from sparse observations while using mechanics to connect the gaps. The learned representation makes that inference fast enough to accompany a live stream of marker measurements.

“Smooth” refers to variation along the arm. The network reconstructs each time frame independently. Its present formulation does not learn temporal dynamics, and the paper leaves dynamic state estimation, more complex motions such as bend propagation, and sensory feedback control as future directions.

The basis, mechanical parameters, marker arrangement, and simulated workspace still shape what can be reconstructed reliably. New deformation patterns or a different robot can require a new basis and training data. Within the evaluated settings, the result is a practical step toward giving soft robots a continuously updated account of their own posture and deformation.

Paper and attribution

This post is based on A Neural Network-Based Framework for Fast and Smooth Posture Reconstruction of a Soft Continuum Arm, by Tixian Wang, Heng-Sheng Chang, Seung Hyun Kim, Jiamiao Guo, Ugur Akcal, Benjamin Walt, Darren Biskup, Udit Halder, Girish Krishnan, Girish Chowdhary, Mattia Gazzola, and Prashant G. Mehta, published in ICRA 2025, pp. 14015–14022. Tixian Wang and Heng-Sheng Chang contributed equally.

The method and results described here follow the published paper. Figures 2–5 are reproduced from the September 19, 2024 arXiv preprint, with explanatory captions supplied here. The figure assets retain the source's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license.

The implementation is available on GitHub. For the optimization method that this work extends, see the earlier post, Seeing How Soft Arms Deform: From Camera Images to Six Strain Fields. The BibTeX below cites the published conference paper.

entry.title: Seeing How Soft Arms Deform: From Camera Images to Six Strain Fields
entry.content:
Take a flexible tube and twist one end. Its center line can remain almost unchanged, even though the material has undergone a substantial deformation. Now bend it while twisting, or let neighboring cross-sections slide sideways relative to one another. A picture of the tube's outline becomes even less informative about what is happening inside its motion.

This is a measurement problem for soft robotics and biomechanics: how can we recover the way a slender body deforms, along its entire length, from a few camera observations?

In our paper, A physics-informed, vision-based method to reconstruct all deformation modes in slender bodies, Seung Hyun Kim, Chia-Hsien Shih, Naveen Kumar Uppalapati, Udit Halder, Girish Krishnan, Prashant G. Mehta, Mattia Gazzola, and I combine multi-camera tracking with Cosserat rod mechanics. The result is an estimate of both the body's three-dimensional pose and its six strain fields, including twist and shear.

The cameras supply discrete observations. Mechanics helps connect them into a continuous body.

Reconstruction in action

A center line is only part of the shape

A Cosserat rod represents a slender body with two ingredients at every location along its length: a position $\mathbf r(s)$ and an orientation $Q(s)$. Here, $s$ labels position along the reference length of the arm. The columns of $Q$ are three perpendicular unit vectors, called directors, attached to each cross-section.

Two directors span the cross-section; the third is perpendicular to it. That third director need not align with the center-line tangent. Their misalignment is precisely what allows the model to describe shear.

The changes in position and orientation are governed by six components:

DeformationComponentsWhat changes locally
Bending$\kappa_1,\kappa_2$Cross-sections rotate about their two transverse axes
Twisting$\kappa_3$Cross-sections rotate about their own normal axis
Shearing$\nu_1,\nu_2$Neighboring cross-sections shift sideways relative to the local frame
Stretching$\nu_3$Separation changes along the cross-section normal; the undeformed value is 1 for a straight, unstretched rod

With $Q$ mapping local coordinates into the laboratory frame, the rod's kinematics can be written as

$$ \frac{d\mathbf r}{ds}=Q\boldsymbol\nu, \qquad \frac{dQ}{ds}=Q[\boldsymbol\kappa]_\times. $$

The notation $[\boldsymbol\kappa]_\times$ denotes the matrix that takes a cross product with $\boldsymbol\kappa$. Given these strain fields and a base pose, we can integrate the equations to reconstruct the rod.

The inverse problem goes the other way: use measured positions and orientations to infer the strains. Tracking cross-section markers makes orientation observable, which is essential for distinguishing a straight, twisted arm from a straight, untwisted one.

From five cameras to discrete poses

Our laboratory setup surrounds the arm with five action cameras recording at 60 frames per second and 1080p. The cameras are arranged so that each tracked marker point is visible in at least two views over the intended motions.

Before tracking the arm, we calibrate the cameras throughout a $40\times30\times40$ cm workspace. Colored flags hang along weighted nylon wires, and moving this grid through the volume provides more than 1,000 reference points. The reported calibration errors are 1.4 mm on average and 2.6 mm at maximum.

After an initial manual selection, Lucas–Kanade optical flow follows marker points through successive images. Direct Linear Transformation (DLT) combines the calibrated views to estimate their three-dimensional coordinates. The cross-section markers then supply discrete position-and-orientation measurements along the arm.

Multiple views also help with occlusion. When a point disappears from one camera but remains visible to others, its reconstructed position predicts where to look for it when it reappears. This depends on sufficient camera coverage; the method cannot observe a marker hidden from every view.

Let mechanics fill the gaps

Directly differentiating noisy pose measurements can produce unreliable strains. Fitting independent rod segments between successive markers also creates a problem: the segments may meet in position and orientation while their strains jump at the boundaries.

We instead optimize a single rod over its full length. Three terms guide the estimate: an elastic energy, a penalty on rapid spatial changes in strain, and a mismatch cost for the measured poses.

Collect the six strains into $\varepsilon=(\boldsymbol\kappa,\boldsymbol\nu)$, and let $\varepsilon^\circ$ be their intrinsic, stress-free values. Using the paper's quadratic elastic model, the objective is

$$ \begin{aligned} J={}&\frac12\int_0^L (\varepsilon-\varepsilon^\circ)^T R(s) (\varepsilon-\varepsilon^\circ)\,ds\\ &+\frac{\chi_u}{2}\int_0^L \left\|\frac{d\varepsilon}{ds}\right\|^2\,ds\\ &+\sum_j\left[ \frac{\chi_r}{2}\|\mathbf r(s_j)-\mathbf r_j\|^2 +\frac{\chi_Q}{2}\|Q(s_j)-Q_j\|_F^2 \right]. \end{aligned} $$

Here, $R(s)$ is the rigidity matrix, $(\mathbf r_j,Q_j)$ are measured poses, and the positive weights $\chi_u,\chi_r,\chi_Q$ balance smoothness and data agreement. The Frobenius norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ measures the orientation-matrix mismatch.

The elastic term gives different deformations a mechanical cost. The strain-gradient term discourages abrupt variation. The measurement term keeps the reconstruction close to the observations without forcing it to pass exactly through noisy data. Together, these terms express what physics-informed reconstruction means in this work: rod kinematics constrain the geometry, and elasticity supplies a mechanical prior.

The key optimization choice is to treat the spatial derivative of strain, $u(s)=d\varepsilon/ds$, as the control variable. Integrating it produces continuous strain fields. With the base pose and base strain specified, the solver repeatedly:

  1. Integrates strain and pose forward from base to tip.
  2. Propagates sensitivity information backward, accounting for the measurement errors at each marker.
  3. Updates $u(s)$ to reduce the objective.

This is optimal control along the arm's spatial coordinate. The pose costates, which carry sensitivity information backward, can be expressed as internal force and moment. The calculation reconstructs an observed configuration; it does not require prescribing the robot's actuator commands or solving a full time-dependent motion model.

Testing what can be recovered

We first generate synthetic rods from known, smoothly varying strain functions. This gives an exact reference for all six strain components, something much harder to obtain on hardware.

For the tested synthetic curves, the reported relative reconstruction errors fall to roughly 1% with five sampled poses and remain around 5% with two. These are results for the chosen smooth strain profiles, rather than a general sampling rule for every possible soft-body shape.

For the first hardware experiment, we use an 18 cm pneumatic BR² arm made from three parallel fiber-reinforced elastomeric actuators: one designed to bend and two to twist in opposite directions. Five cross-section markers provide the observations.

The opening figure shows separate bending, twisting, and combined actuation. The recovered strain profiles identify the dominant deformation in each case. They also reveal smaller accompanying deformations caused by mechanical coupling, fabrication effects, and gravity.

To measure position accuracy independently, the published paper compares reconstruction with electromagnetic sensors at the arm's midsection, three-quarter position, and last-marker tip. Each actuation experiment is repeated eight times. Table I reports:

Actuation conditionMedian position errorMaximum position error
Maximum bending4.15 mm5.43 mm
Maximum twisting2.96 mm4.03 mm
Both4.13 mm5.13 mm

These measurements assess the complete pipeline, including calibration and reconstruction. The median errors are about 3–4 mm on an arm with a 15.9 mm diameter. Although the abstract summarizes accuracy as below 5 mm, the table records some larger errors. These are position errors, not independent measurements of the accuracy of every strain component.

Recovering coupled deformations

The more demanding demonstrations use a two-section BR² arm and a cable-driven arm. Their different designs help test whether the reconstruction can capture several deformation modes at once.

In the 38 cm BR² arm, one section receives a bending command and the other a twisting command. Eleven cross-section markers support reconstruction of all six strain fields. The expected bending and twisting dominate their respective sections, while smaller coupled strains appear elsewhere.

The 35 cm cable-driven arm uses twelve markers and bends its two sections in different directions. Its softer construction and cable routing let its cross-sectional holders tilt away from perpendicular to the center line. The reconstructed shear captures this visible feature of the deformation.

We also perturb the cable-driven arm's measured marker positions with uniform noise of up to 5 mm. Reconstructing again changes the strain fields by about 10% on average in the paper's relative $L_2$ measure. This tests sensitivity to added noise by comparing two reconstructions; it is not a comparison with independently known physical strains.

What this makes measurable

The contribution is a way to turn sparse pose observations into a mechanically informed description of a whole slender body. It brings bending, twist, shear, and stretch into the same reconstruction, so an experiment can ask where each deformation occurs and how they interact.

The approach still depends on camera calibration, visible markers, a suitable rod model, specified base conditions, and choices of stiffness and smoothing weights. Fine spatial features between widely spaced markers may be smoothed away. Recording at 60 frames per second also does not establish that the complete reconstruction runs in real time.

The hardware demonstrations support laboratory characterization of soft robots. Applying the method to biological bodies would require suitable tracking and modeling choices. Within that scope, it provides a useful connection between what cameras can observe and what mechanics needs to explain: both where the body is and how its material deforms along its length.

Paper and attribution

This post is based on A physics-informed, vision-based method to reconstruct all deformation modes in slender bodies, by Seung Hyun Kim, Heng-Sheng Chang, Chia-Hsien Shih, Naveen Kumar Uppalapati, Udit Halder, Girish Krishnan, Prashant G. Mehta, and Mattia Gazzola, published in ICRA 2022, pp. 4810–4817.

The experimental error statistics above follow Table I in the published paper. Figures 2–5 are reproduced from the September 17, 2021 arXiv preprint, with surrounding page text and original captions removed and explanatory captions supplied here. The figure assets retain the source's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license.

The code repository links to demonstration data and identifies its v0.1 version as the code used to reproduce the paper's results. The BibTeX below cites the published conference paper.
